Week 76 Appendix: The Week the Wall Came Down

A single Supreme Court sitting handed the presidency lasting new power while resistance held just enough ground to keep the ledger nearly even.

This week was defined by a landmark Supreme Court term that simultaneously checked and expanded executive power, alongside mounting evidence of systemic self-enrichment and institutional capture by the Trump White House. The Court struck down birthright-citizenship revocation and blocked an unlawful Fed governor removal, but in the same sitting overturned 90-year-old Humphrey's Executor protections, granting the president sweeping removal power over independent agencies—a structural shift toward unitary executive control. Simultaneously, financial disclosures revealed $2.2 billion in Trump family earnings (much from crypto ventures actively deregulated by the administration), a parallel White House-run internet infrastructure bypassing federal privacy law, and a Democratic-authored report alleging systemic corruption in the 250th-anniversary celebration. ICE conducted record-scale arrests, TPS protections were revoked for hundreds of thousands, and journalists and protesters faced detention. Judicial pushback (mail-ballot rulings, geofence warrant protections, USPS injunction) provided partial counterweight.

Power and Authority

  2. Trump ordered reduction of trees in Lafayette Square to match his presidency number: Altering a historic public park to reflect a personal number shows use of executive influence over public spaces for self-focused purposes. (2026-06-28) [single source]
  3.   4. Trump administration dismantled USAID and moved disaster assistance functions under the State Department: Gutting the foreign aid agency and laying off thousands of workers concentrates disaster-response authority and reduces institutional capacity for humanitarian oversight. (2026-06-28)
